Pregnancy

Miscarriage symptoms, bleeding and getting care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Bleeding in pregnancy can be frightening. It can happen in a continuing pregnancy, during a miscarriage or with another condition such as an ectopic pregnancy. Appearance alone cannot tell you which. You deserve prompt assessment, clear information and support without blame.

Possible symptoms and silent pregnancy loss

Possible symptoms include vaginal spotting or heavier bleeding, lower abdominal cramps, back pain, clots, tissue or fluid. A missed miscarriage may cause few or no symptoms and be found on ultrasound. A change in pregnancy symptoms alone does not establish a loss.

Miscarriage terminology and gestational limits differ between countries; most losses occur early. A very early loss may resemble a period, while a later loss can involve more recognisable tissue. Neither the amount nor the appearance reliably shows the pregnancy's outcome or whether treatment is needed.

Blood colour, clots and comparison with a period

Bleeding can look pink, red or brown and may start and stop. Dark blood can reflect older blood, but colour is not a test of safety. Clots or greyish tissue can occur, yet photographs or visual inspection cannot confirm that a miscarriage is complete or exclude an ectopic pregnancy.

An early loss may be heavier, longer or more painful than your usual period, but these patterns overlap. If pregnancy is possible, contact a clinician about unusual bleeding and follow pregnancy-testing advice. Do not assume that an apparent period or passed tissue rules out pregnancy outside the uterus.

How much bleeding and how long?

The course varies with the pregnancy, whether tissue remains and the treatment used. There may be a heavier phase followed by lighter bleeding; spotting can last around two weeks and sometimes longer. There is no universal three-to-five-hour heavy phase or guaranteed two-week endpoint.

Use pads to help observe bleeding and follow your team's written plan. Increasing or persistent bleeding, worsening pain or bleeding that does not start during planned expectant care needs review. Do not wait several hours to meet a pad-count threshold if bleeding is heavy or you feel unwell.

When to get urgent or emergency help

Get emergency care immediately for heavy bleeding that rapidly soaks a pad, severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, marked dizziness, fainting or collapse. These can signal dangerous bleeding or ectopic pregnancy. Do not drive yourself if faint or unwell.

Seek prompt clinical advice for any bleeding in a known or possible pregnancy. Fever, offensive-smelling discharge, increasing pain or feeling increasingly ill needs urgent assessment for infection or other complications. Later-pregnancy bleeding needs maternity assessment rather than assuming an early-loss home-care plan applies.

How a diagnosis is confirmed

Assessment may include your history, examination, a pregnancy test, ultrasound and blood tests measuring hCG. A vaginal ultrasound is commonly used to locate the pregnancy and assess development; it does not cause a miscarriage. One very early scan may be inconclusive, so a carefully timed repeat scan may be necessary.

Last-period dates or one hCG result cannot settle every diagnosis. If the pregnancy location is not yet known, follow-up must continue until the team establishes what has happened. Passing tissue does not by itself exclude an ectopic pregnancy. New or worsening symptoms require earlier care even while awaiting another scan.

Care choices after a confirmed miscarriage

For a stable person with a confirmed early miscarriage, options can include waiting for tissue to pass, prescribed medicines or a procedure to remove tissue. The choice depends on clinical findings, preferences, access and follow-up. Expectant care often begins with a seven-to-fourteen-day review period, not a promise that everything will finish then.

The team can reassess and discuss continuing to wait, medicines or surgery if symptoms persist or the process has not begun. Significant ongoing bleeding, infection or unsuccessful treatment may make a procedure necessary sooner. Suction treatment may use local or general anaesthesia; it has small but real risks, including bleeding, infection, injury or needing further treatment.

Progesterone and cervical stitches are selective treatments

Bleeding with a continuing intrauterine pregnancy is sometimes called threatened miscarriage. Under NICE guidance, vaginal progesterone is offered for early bleeding when a scan confirms an intrauterine pregnancy and there has been a previous miscarriage. It is not a general remedy for all bleeding, a suspected low hormone level or an already confirmed loss.

A cervical stitch may help selected people at risk of late miscarriage or preterm birth because the cervix shortens or opens early. It does not treat most early miscarriages. Infection, bleeding, contractions or broken waters can make it unsuitable, and an emergency stitch has higher risks and cannot guarantee continuation. These treatments require specialist assessment.

Follow-up, testing and physical recovery

Follow the agreed check-up and testing plan. If bleeding has not begun within 48 hours after prescribed misoprostol, contact your treating team; seek help sooner for warning signs. With expectant care, NICE advises a home pregnancy test three weeks after the miscarriage; with medical management, test three weeks after treatment, and seek review if positive. Remaining pregnancy hormone can keep a test positive; it should not simply be dismissed as a false result. Retained tissue, an ectopic or molar pregnancy and other explanations may need assessment.

A negative test does not make heavy bleeding, fever or persistent pelvic pain safe to ignore. Bleeding and discomfort should generally settle; your period may return within four to eight weeks, with variation. Avoid sex until symptoms have resolved and follow your team's advice. Ovulation can occur before the first period, so discuss contraception if you do not want another pregnancy yet.

Causes, future pregnancy and repeated losses

Many early losses result from chance chromosome changes, and often no definite cause is found. Age, uterine differences, antiphospholipid syndrome and some poorly controlled hormonal or medical conditions can affect risk. Ordinary work, usual exercise and sex are not usual causes. Smoking and alcohol can increase risk, but a risk factor never proves that someone caused their loss.

Many people have a successful later pregnancy, including after repeated losses; no percentage can predict an individual outcome. Services use different recurrent-loss definitions, and evaluation may be appropriate after two losses or earlier for particular concerns. Discuss prior history, health and readiness before trying again. After an uncomplicated early loss, a compulsory wait for one period is not universal; complications or a specific diagnosis may require a different plan.

Emotional recovery and practical support

Grief, relief, numbness, anger and mixed feelings can occur, and partners may respond differently. There is no deadline for emotional recovery. Ask your care team for counselling, a loss-support service or help with sleep and daily functioning if you need it.

Accept practical help and arrange a contact you can reach if symptoms change. If planning another pregnancy, review medicines and chronic conditions, avoid smoking and alcohol, and ask about appropriate folic acid. Information can support decisions, but compassionate personalised care is central.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Symptoms alone cannot confirm miscarriage; ultrasound and follow-up may be needed to establish pregnancy location and development.

Care after confirmed loss should include informed choices, a written follow-up plan and clear emergency contacts.

Progesterone, cervical stitches and recurrent-loss investigations have specific indications and require professional assessment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama helps you understand symptoms and prepare questions for care. It cannot diagnose miscarriage, locate a pregnancy, confirm that tissue has passed completely or replace urgent assessment.

When to seek help

Get emergency care now for heavy bleeding, severe abdominal or shoulder-tip pain, fainting or collapse. Seek urgent advice for fever, offensive discharge, worsening pain or feeling ill. Contact a clinician about any bleeding in a known or possible pregnancy, and keep follow-up even if symptoms settle.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Blood colour, clots or tissue cannot diagnose a miscarriage or exclude ectopic pregnancy.
  • Heavy bleeding, severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or collapse needs immediate emergency care.
  • Confirmed early loss may be managed by waiting, prescribed medicines or a procedure, with follow-up.
  • A positive three-week follow-up test or ongoing symptoms needs review; a negative test does not cancel warning signs.
  • Most losses are not caused by something you did, and support and future care should be individualised.

Frequently asked questions

What does miscarriage bleeding look like?

It may be spotting or heavier bleeding with clots or tissue, but a continuing or ectopic pregnancy can also bleed. Appearance alone cannot confirm the diagnosis or completion.

How long does miscarriage bleeding last?

It varies. Lighter bleeding or spotting may last around two weeks or longer depending on management. Follow the clinical plan and seek review for persistent, increasing or concerning symptoms; there is no fixed safe duration.

Does brown, pink or red blood tell me what is happening?

No. Different colours can occur in several situations, and brown blood is not automatically harmless. Seek pregnancy-related bleeding advice regardless of colour.

How much bleeding is too much?

Heavy bleeding that rapidly soaks a pad needs emergency help, especially with severe pain, dizziness or fainting. Do not wait hours for a numerical threshold before seeking care.

Can a miscarriage happen without bleeding?

Yes. A missed miscarriage may have few symptoms and be diagnosed by ultrasound, sometimes with a repeat scan to avoid a premature diagnosis.

Does everyone need a curettage under general anaesthesia?

No. Waiting, medicines or a procedure may be appropriate. Local or general anaesthesia may be available for suction treatment. Clinical urgency, informed choice and the team's advice guide care.

Can I ignore a positive test several weeks after a loss?

No. Hormone can remain detectable, but a positive three-week follow-up test needs review. Heavy bleeding, fever, offensive discharge or persistent pain needs care even with a negative test.

When can I try again, and will it happen again?

Discuss readiness and any complications with your team. Ovulation can return before your period, and waiting one period is not universally required after an uncomplicated early loss. Many later pregnancies succeed, but previous losses, age and health influence individual advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
